What we cover

6 services under Excavation

Each one has its own page. If you are not sure which applies, call and describe what you are looking at.

Volume

Bulk Excavation Childcare centres, unit developments, commercial Large volume, where the cartage rate matters as much as the dig rate. Basement Excavation Residential and commercial basements Bulk and detailed in one dig, usually against a boundary and usually in rock.

Precision

Detailed Excavation Footings, pads, pier holes, lift pits, trenches Precision work to a set out, often after the bulk dig is finished. Site Cut and Levelling Cut and fill, benching, building platforms Cutting a sloping block to the level the design needs, and compacting what is left.

Hard ground and pools

Rock Excavation Sandstone and shale Hammers and rippers. The strongest association we have is the Northern Beaches. Pool Excavation The hole, and getting the spoil out Usually a block with no room, which is what decides the machine and the truck.

Scoping

What decides an excavation price

Volume is only one of six, and it is rarely the one that moves the number most:

  • What the ground is. Clay rips, sandstone needs a hammer, and shale sits between the two. A geotechnical report narrows this a long way; without one the rock is priced on rates rather than a fixed figure.
  • What machine can get in. A block that only takes a mini excavator takes longer and costs more per cubic metre than the same volume on an open site.
  • Where the spoil goes. Clean fill, VENM, mixed material and contaminated soil have different destinations and different rates. The classification is the price, not the volume.
  • What the truck can do at the kerb. If a truck and dog cannot turn or cannot legally stand, the work goes out in bogie tippers, which is more loads for the same volume.
  • What is next door. Excavating against a boundary, a neighbouring footing or a retaining structure changes the method before it changes the price.
  • Water. Groundwater, or a block that holds water after rain, changes both the method and the classification of what comes out.

All six are visible at a site visit, which is why we do one before pricing anything substantial.

What we need to price it properly

The address
So we can look at access and what is around it
What is there now
A photograph from the street and one from the rear
Any reports you hold
Hazardous materials, geotechnical, survey or levels
Your dates
What has to be finished by when, and what is waiting on it

We attend the site before quoting anything substantial. A number sent without a visit is a range with a contingency inside it, and you pay for that either way.

How it runs

How a dig is actually run

The order matters more on a confined block than on an open one.

01

Site visit and set out

Access, levels, what is next door, and where the trucks will stand. The set out comes from your surveyor or engineer, not from us.

02

Services and protection

Underground services located before anything goes in the ground. Sediment control, and protection of the adjoining property where the dig comes near it.

03

Strip and stockpile

Topsoil and overburden off first, stockpiled where there is room and carted straight out where there is not.

04

Bulk dig

The volume, with the method reassessed as the ground changes. On a confined block the trucks line up with the machine rather than the other way round.

05

Detailed work and trim

Footings, pads, pier holes and trenches to the set out, then the base trimmed to level.

06

Compaction and handover

Compacted where that is in scope, left at the level nominated, with the dockets handed over.

Before you book

What people ask about excavation

How do you price rock when nobody knows how much is there?
By separating what is known from what is not. The strip, the access and the cartage come from a site visit. The rock is priced by the cubic metre at a rate agreed before we start, so you are not exposed to a guess. A geotechnical report narrows the range considerably.
Do you locate the services?
Underground services are located before anything goes in the ground. What we cannot do is take responsibility for a service that is not where the plan says it is, which is why the locate happens on site rather than on paper.
Can you excavate right up to the boundary?
That depends on what is on the other side of it and on what the engineer has specified. Shoring, piling and underpinning are engineered by others; we coordinate the dig around them rather than designing them.
What about the water table?
If the dig goes below it, dewatering is a separate scope with its own approval and its own discharge requirements. It is better to know before the hole is open than after.
Do you do the compaction as well?
Where it is in scope, yes, in layers rather than one pass. Fill that was tipped and spread rather than placed and compacted is where a slab finds a soft spot later.
Can the demolition and the dig be the same contract?
Yes, and on a knockdown rebuild that is usually the point. One mobilisation instead of two is the single biggest saving available on a confined block.

A site plan or an engineer’s levels, plus a picture of the driveway and the street, decides most of an excavation price. A geotechnical report, if one exists, narrows the rock a long way.
